content: On this I awakened, and saw; and my sleep was sweet to me. {{v:27}} “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man and with the seed of animal. {{v:28}} It will happen that, like as I have watched over them to pluck up and to break down and to overthrow and to destroy and to afflict, so I will watch over them to build and to plant,” says the LORD. {{v:29}} “In those days they will say no more, “‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge.’ {{v:30}} But everyone will die for his own iniquity. Every man who eats the sour grapes, his teeth will be set on edge. {{v:31}} “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah, {{v:32}} not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt, which covenant of mine they broke, although I was a husband to them,” says the LORD. {{v:33}} “But this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days,” says the LORD: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart. I will be their God, and they shall be my people. {{v:34}} They will no longer each teach his neighbor, and every man teach his brother, saying, ‘Know the LORD;’ for they will all know me, from their least to their greatest,” says the LORD, “for I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.” {{v:35}} The LORD, who gives the sun for a light by day, and the ordinances of the moon and of the stars for a light by night, who stirs up the sea, so that its waves roar— the LORD of Armies is his name, says: {{v:36}} “If these ordinances depart from before me,” says the LORD, “then the offspring of Israel also will cease from being a nation before me forever.” {{v:37}} The LORD says: “If heaven above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth searched out beneath, then I will also cast off all the offspring of Israel for all that they have done,” says the LORD. {{v:38}} “Behold, the days come,” says the LORD, “that the city will be built to the LORD from the tower of Hananel to the gate of the corner. {{v:39}} The measuring line will go out further straight onward to the hill Gareb, and will turn toward Goah. {{v:40}} The whole valley of the dead bodies and of the ashes, and all the fields to the brook Kidron, to the corner of the horse gate toward the east, will be holy to the LORD. It will not be plucked up or thrown down any more forever.”

facets.text: God promises to reverse the long work of judgment: the same vigilant care He exercised to "pluck up" and "overthrow" He will now exercise "to build and to plant." The verbs of destruction from Jeremiah's original commission are deliberately answered by verbs of restoration, showing that God's judgment was never His final word but served a redemptive purpose. Divine watchfulness is constant; its direction turns from tearing down to building up once the purification is complete.
facets.question: Why does God allow destruction before restoration in His dealings with His people?

facets.text: The old proverb that children suffer for their fathers' sins is abolished in favor of personal moral responsibility: "everyone will die for his own iniquity." This does not deny the solidarity of sin but corrects a fatalism that excused personal guilt by blaming ancestors. It anticipates the maturing moral consciousness that each soul stands accountable before God for its own choices.
facets.question: Are we punished for the sins of our ancestors or only for our own?

facets.text: The heart of the passage is the promise of a New Covenant, unlike the Sinai covenant Israel broke though God had been a faithful "husband" to them. Catholic tradition reads this as fulfilled in Christ, who at the Last Supper declared the cup "the new covenant in my blood," and the Letter to the Hebrews cites this very text to show the old covenant's obsolescence. The nuptial imagery reveals that covenant is not mere contract but a spousal bond of love that human infidelity wounds but divine fidelity restores.
facets.question: What is the new covenant God promised through the prophets and how is it fulfilled?

facets.text: The distinctive gift of the New Covenant is interior: God will write His law "in their inward parts" and "on their heart" rather than on tablets of stone. This points to the grace of the Holy Spirit poured into believers, transforming obedience from external command into an inward inclination toward the good. What the Law demanded from without, grace now accomplishes from within, so that righteousness flows from a renewed heart.
facets.question: What does it mean that God writes his law on our hearts?

facets.text: In the New Covenant "they will all know me, from their least to their greatest," a universal and immediate knowledge of God not dependent on being taught. This does not abolish teaching but describes the intimate personal knowledge of God given through the indwelling Spirit, a knowledge open to every rank without distinction. It foreshadows the universal call to communion with God fulfilled in the Church.
facets.question: What kind of knowledge of God does the new covenant promise to everyone?

facets.text: The New Covenant is grounded in the definitive forgiveness of sins: "I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more." This total remission, which the sacrifices of the old law could not achieve, is accomplished by the once-for-all sacrifice of Christ. God's forgetting of sin is not divine amnesia but the reality of a debt fully cancelled, restoring the sinner to unbroken communion.
facets.question: How completely does God forgive and forget our sins under the new covenant?

facets.text: God pledges the permanence of His people by binding it to the fixed ordinances of creation: only if the sun, moon, and stars fail will Israel cease to be a nation. The Creator who governs the cosmos guarantees His covenant with the same unbreakable fidelity, so that His saving purpose is as sure as the order of the heavens. This assurance grounds hope not in human constancy but in God's own unchanging will.
facets.question: How certain is God's faithfulness to his covenant people?

facets.text: The oracle closes with the promise of a rebuilt and consecrated city, where even the valley of dead bodies and ashes—defiled ground of judgment—will become "holy to the LORD" and never again uprooted. What was a place of death is transfigured into sacred space, prefiguring the heavenly Jerusalem and the sanctification of all that sin had corrupted. God's restoration reaches even the ruined and unclean, making them holy forever.
facets.question: How can places marked by death and defilement become holy to God?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Jeremiah 31:26–40 proclaims the New Covenant—interior law, universal knowledge of God, and definitive forgiveness—grounded in God's creational fidelity, alongside restored personal responsibility and the consecration of a rebuilt Jerusalem.

[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: God turns His vigilant work from plucking up and destroying to building and planting, showing judgment served restoration.
[MORAL | explicit]: The proverb of sour grapes is abolished; each person dies for his own iniquity, affirming personal moral accountability.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The New Covenant, unlike the broken Sinai covenant, is fulfilled in Christ's blood at the Last Supper and cited in Hebrews; spousal imagery reveals covenant as nuptial bond.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The law written on the heart signifies the interior grace of the Holy Spirit transforming obedience from without to within.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The promise that all will know God, least to greatest, describes intimate Spirit-given knowledge fulfilled in the Church.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Total forgiveness—God remembering sin no more—achieved by Christ's once-for-all sacrifice, cancelling the debt fully.
[SCRIPTURAL | explicit]: God binds His people's permanence to the fixed cosmic ordinances, grounding covenant fidelity in creation's order.
[TYPOLOGICAL | inferential]: The rebuilt city, even defiled ground of death, becomes holy forever, prefiguring the heavenly Jerusalem and sanctified creation.
